source.title: Steering from Random Quotients: A Sample-Complexity Theory of Polysemantic Contrast Pairs
source.authors: Khanh Nguyen Quoc; Luong Doan; D. Nguyen; M. Hung; N. Vũ; Phong Ho; N. Duong; T. Do

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses polysemantic coactivation as motivation for a quotient-based steering method, but its experiments assess steering-vector recovery and behavior, not whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or how common such neurons are.
record.gate_note: The paper reports synthetic, public-data, and Pythia quotient-recovery results, plus TruthfulQA steering results. These evaluate steering estimators and contrast-pair confounding, not neuron polysemanticity or the claim versions. The neuron and superposition findings in related work are cited, not newly tested. The selected validation configurations are not outcomes about the claim.
record.test_reason: The paper uses 'polysemanticity' loosely to describe contrast pairs that coactivate a target concept with nuisance features. It builds and evaluates a quotient-based steering estimator (QLS, Sparse-Steer) on synthetic, TF-IDF and Pythia-410M data. It reports no neuron-level activation analysis, no share of polysemantic neurons, and no test of superposition, training causes, architecture effects or measurement dependence. Superposition and SAE work are cited only as motivation (Related Work). It therefore relies on the idea and reports only its own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors frame the work as a conditional theory of steering-direction recovery given credible nuisance supports. Quotienting reduces nuisance leakage, while raw margin can favour the style-entangled DiM vector. The public-data and Pythia pilots do not validate a semantic target. The paper makes no neuron-level polysemanticity claims.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops quotient least squares and sparse steering for contrast-derived steering vectors; it does not apply the original neuron-response or feature-interpretation methods from the cited sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with coactivation probability and sample size in synthetic recovery experiments, with heuristic support construction across public-data pilots, and with the steering objective in the counter-confounder experiment: DiM has higher raw margin, while QLS has lower style leakage and a smaller angle to the operational target.

fits_no_version.finding: In the controlled TruthfulQA counter-confounder test on Pythia-410M, DiM had the higher reversed-style margin (-0.081 vs -0.207 for QLS). DiM also had style cosine 0.500 versus about 0 for QLS, and a larger angle to the prefix-balanced target (0.825 vs 0.589).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quotienting out an estimated nuisance span removes injected style leakage from contrast-derived steering vectors, at a cost in raw behavioural margin.

fits_no_version.finding: In the validation-selected TruthfulQA sweep, both methods improved the no-steer margin of -0.502 (DiM -0.262, QLS -0.273). Accuracy was similar (0.419 vs 0.416).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: QLS steering does not outperform difference-in-means on raw TruthfulQA margin or accuracy in Pythia-410M.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The paper states that public-data and Pythia support constructions are heuristic and do not establish an externally validated semantic target. The controlled target is operational rather than absolute semantic ground truth. Language-model experiments are narrow, using Pythia-410M on TruthfulQA; Table 2 reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No neuron-level results are reported. Synthetic and public-data quotient-recovery angles, sparse-steering results, and other estimator diagnostics were left out because they measure recovery or performance of steering estimators rather than neuron polysemanticity. They appear in Sections 6.1–6.2 and Table 1.

untested.parts: No vision models or neuron responses examined.
No count or layer distribution of polysemantic MLP neurons; Pythia hidden states are randomly projected to 192 dimensions and used only for steering-vector estimation.
Superposition (Elhage et al., 2022) is cited as motivation for the nuisance model, not tested.
No study of initialization, regularization or training noise.
No comparison across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
No neuron-level reinterpretation of polysemantic neurons.
No analysis of how polysemanticity classification depends on activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none'] and cannot_determine. 'Polysemantic' in the title refers to contrast pairs coactivating nuisance features in activation space, not to individual neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The quotient-recovery angles in Table 1 are correctly left out as estimator-performance results. No verdict labels are given.

versions.untested_parts: No neuron-level response measurements in image classifiers or other vision models.
No measurement of the share or layer distribution of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models.
No test of whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings.
No neuron-level interpretation test for shared features, related jobs, or truly unrelated mixtures.
No test of how neuron polysemanticity classifications vary with activation range or explanation-scoring method.
